My husband and I have three children and I have been a stay at home mom for 10 years. My oldest daughter is 11. My husband's 16 year old daughter from a previous marriage wants to babysit for us. If we pay her to babysit can be we qualify for the dependent care credit?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	You may be able to claim the child and dependent care credit if you paid expenses for the care of a
     2	qualifying individual to enable you (and your spouse, if filing a joint return) to work or actively
     3	look for work. Generally, you may not take this credit if your filing status is married filing
     4	separately. However, see What's Your Filing Status? in Publication 503, Child and Dependent Care
     5	Expenses, which describes an exception for certain taxpayers living apart from their spouse and
     6	meeting other requirements. The amount of the credit is a percentage of the amount of work-related
     7	expenses you paid to a care provider for the care of a qualifying individual. The percentage depends
     8	on your adjusted gross income.
     9	
    10	
    11	 Dollar limit
    12	 The total expenses that you may use to calculate the credit may not be more than $3,000 (for one
    13	qualifying individual) or $6,000 (for two or more qualifying individuals). Expenses paid for the
    14	care of a qualifying individual are eligible expenses if the primary reason for paying the expense
    15	is to assure the individual's well-being and protection. If you received dependent care benefits
    16	that you exclude or deduct from your income, you must subtract the amount of those benefits from the
    17	dollar limit that applies to you.
    18	
    19	
    20	 Qualifying individual
    21	 A qualifying individual for the child and dependent care credit is:
    22	
    23	
    24	 Your dependent qualifying child who was under age 13 when the care was provided,
    25	 Your spouse who was physically or mentally incapable of self-care and lived with you for more than
    26	half of the year, or
    27	 An individual who was physically or mentally incapable of self-care, lived with you for more than
    28	half of the year, and either: (a) was your dependent; or (b) could have been your dependent except
    29	that he or she received gross income of $4,700 or more, or filed a joint return, or you (or your
    30	spouse, if filing jointly) could have been claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer's 2023 return.
    31	 Physically or mentally not able to care for oneself - An individual is physically or mentally
    32	incapable of self-care if, as a result of a physical or mental defect, the individual is incapable
    33	of caring for his or her hygiene or nutritional needs or requires the full-time attention of another
    34	person for the individual's own safety or the safety of others.
    35	
    36	
    37	 Children of divorced or separated parents or parents living apart - A noncustodial parent who is
    38	claiming a child as a dependent should review the rules under the topic Child of divorced or
    39	separated parents or parents living apart in Publication 503, because a child may be treated as the
    40	qualifying individual of the custodial parent for the child and dependent care credit, even if the
    41	noncustodial parent is entitled to claim the child as a dependent.
    42	
    43	
    44	 Individual qualifying for part of year - If an individual is a qualifying individual for only a
    45	part of the tax year, only those expenses paid for care of the individual during that part of the
    46	year are included in calculating the credit.
    47	
    48	
    49	 Taxpayer identification number (TIN) - You must provide the TIN (usually the Social Security
    50	number) of each qualifying individual.
    51	
    52	
    53	 Care of a qualifying individual
    54	 The care may be provided in the household or outside the household; however, don't include any
    55	amounts that aren't primarily for the well-being of the individual. You should divide the expenses
    56	between amounts that are primarily for the care of the individual and amounts that aren't primarily
    57	for the care of the individual. You must reduce the expenses primarily for the care of the
    58	individual by the amount of any dependent care benefits provided by your employer that you exclude
    59	from gross income. In general, you can exclude up to $5,000 for dependent care benefits received
    60	from your employer. Additionally, in general, the expenses claimed may not exceed the smaller of
    61	your earned income or your spouse's earned income. If you or your spouse is a full-time student or
    62	incapable of self-care, then you or your spouse is treated as having earned income for each month
    63	that you or your spouse is a full-time student or incapable of self-care. Your or your spouse's
    64	earned income for each month is $250 if there is one qualifying person ($500 if two or more
    65	qualifying individuals). See the topic Earned Income Limit in Publication 503 PDF for further
    66	information.
    67	
    68	
    69	 Care providers
    70	 You must identify all persons or organizations that provide care for your child or dependent. You
    71	must report the name, address, and TIN (either the Social Security number or the employer
    72	identification number) of the care provider on your return. If the care provider is a tax-exempt
    73	organization, you need only report the name and address of the organization on your return. You can
    74	use Form W-10, Dependent Care Provider's Identification and Certification to request this
    75	information from the care provider. If you can't provide information regarding the care provider,
    76	you may still be eligible for the credit if you can show that you exercised due diligence in
    77	attempting to provide the required information. If you pay a provider to care for your dependent or
    78	spouse in your home, you may be a household employer. If you're a household employer, you may have
    79	to withhold and pay Social Security and Medicare taxes and pay federal unemployment tax. For more
    80	information, refer to Do You Have Household Employees? in Publication 503, Publication 926,
    81	Household Employer's Tax Guide, or Topic no. 756.
    82	
    83	
    84	 Payments to relatives or dependents - The care provider can't be your spouse, the parent of your
    85	qualifying individual if your qualifying individual is your child and under age 13, your child who
    86	is under the age of 19, or a dependent whom you or your spouse may claim on your return.
    87	
    88	
    89	 Reporting on your tax return
    90	 If you qualify for the credit, complete Form 2441, Child and Dependent Care Expenses and attach to
    91	Form 1040, U.S Individual Income Tax Return, Form 1040-SR, U.S. Tax Return for Seniors or Form
    92	1040-NR, U.S. Nonresident Alien Income Tax Return. If you received dependent care benefits from your
    93	employer (an amount is shown on your Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement), you must complete Part III
    94	of Form 2441.
    95	
    96	
    97	 Additional information
    98	 For more information, refer to Am I eligible to claim the child and dependent care credit?

Based on the document in `doc.txt`, the answer is **no, you would not qualify for the child and dependent care credit**, for the following reasons:

**1. You are not working (or actively looking for work).**
The document states that you may claim the credit only if you paid for care of a qualifying individual "to enable you (and your spouse, if filing a joint return) to work or actively look for work." As a stay-at-home mom for 10 years, you are not working or actively looking for work.

**2. The earned-income limit would reduce your credit to zero.**
The document states that "the expenses claimed may not exceed the smaller of your earned income or your spouse's earned income." Because you have no earned income (you are a stay-at-home mom), the smaller of the two earned incomes is $0, so the amount of expenses you could claim is $0. (The document only provides an exception treating a spouse as having earned income of $250/month if that spouse is a full-time student or incapable of self-care, which does not apply to you.)

**3. The 16-year-old may be disqualified as a care provider.**
The document states that "the care provider can't be your spouse, the parent of your qualifying individual if your qualifying individual is your child and under age 13, your child who is under the age of 19, or a dependent whom you or your spouse may claim on your return." The 16-year-old is not your child, so the "child under 19" restriction does not apply to her. However, **if she is a dependent whom you or your husband may claim on your return, she cannot be a care provider** for the credit. The document does not tell us whether she is your dependent, so this depends on your specific situation.

**Note on your 11-year-old daughter:** She would qualify as a "qualifying individual" (a dependent qualifying child under age 13), so the problem is not the child being cared for — it is your lack of earned income and the potential disqualification of the 16-year-old as a care provider.

In summary, even if you paid the 16-year-old to babysit, you would not qualify for the credit because you are not working or actively looking for work, and the earned-income limit (the smaller of your earned income or your spouse's earned income) would be $0 given that you have no earned income.
